items.prompt: Two implementations of the same function both pass every test. What does this tell you about their design quality (coupling, cohesion, future change cost)?
choices: Passing tests proves both have equally good design
Nothing directly — correctness (does it produce the right output) and design quality (how much future changes will cost) are different properties; code can be fully correct and still badly designed
Passing tests proves the better-designed one is faster
Design quality can only be assessed by counting lines of code
items.explanation: Correctness and design quality are separate properties. Tests verify output for given inputs, not how expensive the next change will be. Both L3 notification-service versions are equally correct; they differ sharply in what adding a channel costs.
items.reference:
✅ Correctness

right output, tested inputs

📈 Design quality

cost of the next change

Why: code can score perfectly on one and terribly on the other.
items.learnMore:
Correctness vs. design quality

A test suite asks one question: for the inputs I tried, did I get the right output? Design quality asks a completely different one: when the next requirement arrives, how much of this code has to be understood and touched to satisfy it? A function can be 100% correct today and still be the most expensive part of the codebase to change tomorrow — the L1 checkout example passed every test in month 1 and in month 6, and still took 3 weeks instead of 2 hours the second time.

Common mistake

Treating "all tests pass" as evidence the code is well designed. Tests verify behavior for the cases someone thought to write — they say nothing about how entangled the code is with the rest of the system, which is what actually determines future cost.

items.prompt: A checkout function passes every test in month 1 and still passes every test in month 6, yet a same-sized change takes 2 hours in month 1 and 3 weeks in month 6. What does this gap show?
choices: The test suite must be broken, since correctness should predict change cost
The tests were measuring design quality, not correctness, all along
Correctness held steady across both months while design quality — a separate property governing future change cost — had degraded, and no test suite would have caught that
Three weeks is simply how long any change to production code should take
items.explanation: This is the L1 scenario exactly: the code never stopped being correct. What changed was invisible to any test — the accumulated coupling and lost cohesion underneath it, which only shows up as cost when someone actually tries to change it.

choices: Because badly designed code always fails its tests immediately

Because a test suite (and a first read of the code) can confirm correctness today, but the cost design quality imposes only shows up later, when someone tries to change the code — and often not the same person who wrote it

items.prompt: What does "high coupling" between two pieces of code mean?
choices: They are stored in the same file
They are entangled such that changing one is likely to force changes in the other, often because one reaches into the other's internal implementation details rather than a stable interface
They share a common naming convention
They were written by the same developer
items.explanation: Coupling measures entanglement, not proximity or authorship. OrderService reaching into EmailService's smtp_client internals means a change to EmailService's implementation can break OrderService even though OrderService's own job never changed.
items.reference:
🔗 High coupling

reaches into another module's internals

🧩 Low coupling

depends on a narrow, stable interface

Why: coupling measures entanglement, not proximity.
items.learnMore:
Coupling

Coupling is how much one piece of code's correctness depends on the internal details of another. L2's example has OrderService reach into EmailService.smtp_client directly — any change to how EmailService is built internally can now break OrderService, even though nothing about completing an order changed. The fix isn't "talk to it less" but "talk to it through a narrower, more stable surface" — a .notify(order) method instead of a concrete SMTP client.

Common mistake

Assuming coupling is about how many modules a class talks to. It's about how much of what it talks to it depends on — a class can call ten well-abstracted interfaces with low coupling, or reach into one module's internals with high coupling.

items.prompt: OrderService is rewritten to depend only on `notifier.notify(order)` instead of a concrete EmailService's internals. What has changed about its coupling?
choices: Nothing — coupling is fixed once code is written
Coupling decreased: the set of changes to the notifier that could break OrderService shrank from "almost anything internal" to "changing what .notify() means"
Coupling increased, because OrderService now depends on an interface instead of a concrete class
Coupling is unrelated to what a class depends on
items.explanation: Depending on a stable, narrow interface is exactly how coupling is reduced — not by depending on nothing, but by depending on less, and on something less likely to change.

items.prompt: What does low cohesion in a single class or module mean?
choices: The class has too few public methods
The class bundles multiple responsibilities that each have an independent reason to change, so an unrelated change to one risks affecting the others
The class is stored in the wrong folder
The class doesn't use inheritance
items.explanation: Low cohesion is about mixed reasons to change, not file organization or API surface size. A class combining pricing, email, and logging logic forces a pricing bug fix and an email-copy tweak into the same file.
items.reference:
🧩 Low cohesion

bundles unrelated reasons to change

🧠 High cohesion

one module, one reason to change

Why: the test is shared reason to change, not shared subject matter.
items.learnMore:
Cohesion

Cohesion is whether a module's responsibilities genuinely belong together. L2's OrderProcessor has three methods that all touch order — that looks related, but pricing logic, email copy, and analytics schema are three independent reasons to change, so bundling them is still low cohesion. Splitting into PricingCalculator, OrderNotifier, and AnalyticsLogger means a change to one can never accidentally introduce a bug in the other two.

Common mistake

Judging cohesion by whether methods touch the same data. Two methods can both take the same argument and still have nothing to do with each other's reason for existing.

items.prompt: A class has ten methods, and all ten operate on the same `Order` object. Does that guarantee good cohesion?
choices: Yes — operating on the same object is the definition of cohesion
No — cohesion depends on whether those methods share a reason to change, not just a shared data type; unrelated responsibilities can all touch the same object and still be low-cohesion
No, because good cohesion requires exactly one method per class
Yes, but only if the class name contains the word "Manager"
items.explanation: Shared subject matter (all touching `Order`) is not the same as shared reason to change. Pricing, notification, and analytics logic can all take an `Order` argument while still being three independent concerns that shouldn't live together.
items.reference:

bundles unrelated reasons to change

🧠 High cohesion

one module, one reason to change

items.prompt: Why does the "technical debt" metaphor work as a description of a deliberate shortcut in code?
choices: Because shortcuts always cost literal money to fix later

Because, like financial debt, a deliberate shortcut can be a reasonable trade if paid down deliberately, but the same shortcut left unaddressed accrues "interest" — every change built on top of it gets more expensive
Because "debt" just means any code a reviewer doesn't like
Because technical debt, unlike financial debt, never has to be repaid
items.explanation: The metaphor's power is the compounding structure: debt paid down deliberately is a manageable trade; debt left unaddressed grows more expensive to fix the longer it's carried, exactly like accruing interest.
items.reference:
💵 Financial debt

deliberate loan + interest if unpaid

⏳ Technical debt

deliberate shortcut + compounding cost if unpaid

Why: a shortcut paid down deliberately is a trade; left unaddressed, it compounds.
items.learnMore:
Technical debt as a metaphor

The metaphor works because both kinds of debt share the same structure: taking a shortcut now (borrowing money, or shipping a coupled quick version) is fine on its own — it's a genuine trade, not automatically a mistake. What makes it dangerous is leaving it unaddressed: every change built on top of an unpaid shortcut gets a little more expensive, the same way unpaid interest compounds a loan.

Common mistake

Treating "technical debt" as a synonym for "bad code," full stop. L3 is explicit: a deliberate shortcut with a plan to revisit it is a reasonable trade. The metaphor's whole point is that the debt itself isn't the problem — leaving it unpaid while more gets built on top of it is.

items.prompt: A team ships a tightly-coupled quick version deliberately, to hit a real deadline, with a concrete plan to revisit it next sprint. Per this unit, is that a mistake?
choices: Yes — any coupling introduced on purpose is always a design failure
Not necessarily — a deliberate shortcut taken to hit a real deadline, with an intent to pay it down, is a reasonable trade; the risk is in leaving it unaddressed while more gets built on top of it
Yes, because deadlines should never affect design decisions
No, because deadlines always justify permanent shortcuts
items.explanation: This is exactly the distinction L3's failure modes draw: technical debt is not inherently bad or inherently fine — a deliberate, tracked shortcut with a payoff plan is different from the same shortcut left to accrue interest for years.

items.prompt: Why is it so easy to under-invest in design quality when writing new code?
choices: Because design quality never actually affects anything measurable
Because the cost of bad design is almost always invisible at write time and only shows up later as a tax on future changes — often paid by someone other than who wrote it
Because good design always takes exactly the same amount of time as bad design
Because most codebases are rewritten before design quality matters
items.explanation: The deferred, diffuse nature of the cost is the whole mechanism: it doesn't show up in code review or in the test suite, only later, when a change has to route around the accumulated entanglement.
items.reference:
Write time: cost hidden→Change time: cost paid

Why: the person who skips design rarely pays for it themselves, and even when they do, it's deferred.
items.learnMore:
Why bad design is easy to under-invest in

A coupled, low-cohesion version of a function often looks identical to a well-designed one from the outside on day one — same inputs, same outputs, same passing tests. The cost only becomes visible when someone tries to change it, which might be months later, and might be a different engineer entirely. That gap between when the shortcut is taken and when its cost is paid is exactly why it's structurally easy to under-invest in design: the incentive to do it well is diffuse and delayed, not immediate.

items.prompt: An engineer ships a coupled, low-cohesion version of a feature and leaves the team before anyone has to change it again. What does this scenario illustrate?
choices: That the coupled version was actually fine, since no cost was ever paid
That the cost of bad design can be deferred onto someone else entirely, which is exactly why the person who introduces it doesn't always feel the consequence
That design quality only matters if the same person maintains the code forever
That leaving a team erases the cost of any design decisions made
items.explanation: The cost doesn't disappear — it's inherited by whoever touches the code next. This is precisely why bad design is easy to under-invest in: the person cutting the corner and the person paying for it are often different people.
items.reference:

Why: the person who skips design rarely pays for it themselves, and even when they do, it's deferred.

No — over-engineering for hypothetical future requirements is its own real cost; the actual skill is judging how much design investment a piece of code is worth given how much it's actually expected to change
Yes, but only for code written by junior engineers
No, because abstraction should never be used under any circumstances
items.explanation: The unit explicitly rejects "always abstract more" as the takeaway. Design investment should track expected future change, not be applied uniformly regardless of whether that change is likely.
items.reference:
This unit is not "always maximize abstraction." Over-engineering for hypothetical future requirements is its own real cost.

Why: the actual skill is matching design investment to expected future change.
items.learnMore:
Design investment is a judgment call, not a maximum

It's tempting to read "bad design is expensive" as "therefore, always build the most decoupled, most abstracted version possible." That's wrong in the other direction: an abstraction built for a change that never arrives is pure cost with zero payoff. The actual skill this unit teaches is judging how much design investment a given piece of code is worth, based on how much — and how unpredictably — it's actually expected to change.

items.prompt: Per L2's cost curve, why do the poorly-designed and well-designed lines start at roughly the same cost for early changes, then diverge later?
choices: Early changes are always trivial regardless of design, so the divergence is an illusion

Bad design's cost compounds — each change has to work around entanglement left by every previous change — while well-designed code's structure doesn't actively fight the next change, keeping cost closer to flat over time
The well-designed version is simply written by more experienced developers
The curves only diverge if the codebase changes programming languages
items.explanation: This is exactly why bad design's cost is easy to miss upfront: it's invisible on the first few changes and only becomes visible as accumulated entanglement makes each subsequent change more expensive than the last — a compounding effect, not a one-time cost.
items.reference:
Change 1–5: both designs cost about the same
Change 20+: poor design compounds, good design stays near-flat

Why: bad design's cost is invisible early and compounds later.
items.learnMore:
Why the curves diverge

Both lines in L2's chart start at roughly the same cost, because early changes haven't yet built up much entanglement to work around. The poorly-designed line curves upward because each new change has to route around every previous change's mess, on top of its own inherent cost — a compounding effect. The well-designed line stays closer to linear because the code's structure isn't actively fighting the next person; each change costs roughly what the last one did.

items.prompt: If you only ever measured the cost of the very first change made to two differently-designed codebases, would you be able to tell which design was better?

Yes, because poorly designed code always fails on the very first change
No measurement of change cost can ever reveal design quality
items.explanation: This is the trap that makes bad design easy to miss: judging design quality from one early change is unreliable, because the compounding effect that separates the two curves hasn't had a chance to show up yet.

How coupling and cohesion combine

Every future change to a codebase has two jobs: figure out what else might be affected, and touch only what's actually relevant. High coupling makes the first job harder (dependents reach past stable interfaces into internals, so "what's affected" balloons). Low cohesion makes the second job harder (unrelated logic is tangled into the same unit, so "only what's relevant" is hard to isolate). Neither property causes bugs directly — they multiply the cost and risk of every subsequent change, which is the actual mechanism behind the diverging cost curve.

Only low cohesion affects bug risk; coupling is purely a performance concern
items.explanation: L2 is precise about the mechanism: coupling and cohesion problems don't themselves produce incorrect output — they raise the cost and risk of the changes layered on top, which is where bugs then have more room to slip in.

items.prompt: Why does depending on "anything with a `.notify(order)` method" reduce coupling compared to depending on a concrete `EmailService`?
choices: Because interfaces are always faster at runtime than concrete classes
Because it narrows what OrderService actually needs to be true about its dependency down to one method's meaning, instead of an entire concrete class's internal structure
Because it means OrderService no longer needs any dependency at all
Because .notify() is a shorter method name than the alternatives
items.explanation: The size of an interface is the size of the promise a dependency makes. `.notify(order)` is a much smaller promise than "here's my whole internal structure," so far fewer future changes to the dependency can break the caller.
items.reference:
.notify(order) is the entire surface OrderService depends on — any object with that one method works.

Why: a narrow, stable interface is what actually shrinks the break-surface.
items.learnMore:
Coupling

Coupling is how much one piece of code's correctness depends on the internal details of another. L2's example has OrderService reach into EmailService.smtp_client directly — any change to how EmailService is built internally can now break OrderService, even though nothing about completing an order changed. The fix isn't "talk to it less" but "talk to it through a narrower, more stable surface" — a .notify(order) method instead of a concrete SMTP client.

Common mistake

Assuming coupling is about how many modules a class talks to. It's about how much of what it talks to it depends on — a class can call ten well-abstracted interfaces with low coupling, or reach into one module's internals with high coupling.

No, because OrderService can only ever support exactly two notifiers

items.prompt: Implement `completeOrder(order, notifiers)` in the decoupled style from L3: it should call `.notify(order)` on every notifier in the `notifiers` array (in order) and return an array of their return values — `OrderService` itself should never need to know how many notifiers there are or what they do.

with zero notifiers, returns an empty array without erroring

items.explanation: OrderService-equivalent code only ever calls the shared `.notify(order)` interface — it never inspects what kind of notifier it's talking to or how many there are. Adding a new notifier type (SMS, push, Slack) never requires touching this function again, which is the entire point of the decoupled design from L3: the change is additive, not invasive.

items.prompt: Implement `registerNotifier(notifiers, notifier)`: it should return a *new* array containing all of `notifiers` plus `notifier` appended at the end, without mutating the original `notifiers` array.

tests.description: appends the new notifier to the end
works when starting from an empty array
does not mutate the original array

items.learnMore:
Conforming to the notifier interface

Because JavaScript (like most dynamically-typed languages) uses structural typing for this kind of interface, any object exposing a `.notify(order)` method can be dropped into the `notifiers` array — no explicit `implements` declaration or shared base class needed. items.prompt: A system will only ever need one notification channel, with no plausible future requirement for a second. Per L3's failure modes, is building the pluggable `notifiers` array abstraction upfront still a good idea?
choices: Yes — more abstraction is always safer, regardless of actual need
No — with no real second channel expected, the abstraction is pure cost with no payoff; the decoupled design is only worth its complexity because a second channel was a real, concrete requirement
Yes, because it makes the code shorter
No, because pluggable abstractions are always a code smell in every context
items.explanation: L3 explicitly calls this over-engineering: design investment should match expected future change, not be applied uniformly regardless of whether that change is actually likely. Building for a hypothetical second channel that never arrives just adds indirection with no corresponding benefit.

abstraction pays for itself

items.learnMore:
When decoupling isn't worth it

The `notifiers` array abstraction earned its complexity in L3 specifically because a second channel (SMS) was a real, concrete requirement that actually arrived. If a system will only ever have one notification channel, building that same abstraction ahead of time is pure cost — extra indirection, an extra file, a slightly harder-to-follow call path — with no future change ever showing up to pay it back. Three similar lines of straightforward code beat a premature interface.

items.prompt: A tightly-coupled quick version of the notification logic is shipped deliberately to hit a real deadline, with a plan to revisit it next sprint. Two years later, it's still there and three more channels have been bolted onto it the same way. What changed between these two moments?
choices: Nothing — technical debt is always equally bad regardless of how long it's carried

The debt went from a reasonable, deliberate trade to unaddressed debt that's accrued real interest — every channel added on top made the eventual refactor more expensive than it would have been the second time it needed to change
The code became more correct over the two years
The debt automatically resolved itself once the deadline passed
items.explanation: This is L3's core distinction: the shortcut itself wasn't the mistake — leaving it unaddressed while more got built on top of it, compounding the eventual cost, is what turned a reasonable trade into real debt.
items.reference:
💵 Financial debt

deliberate loan + interest if unpaid

⏳ Technical debt

deliberate shortcut + compounding cost if unpaid

Why: a shortcut paid down deliberately is a trade; left unaddressed, it compounds.
items.learnMore:
Deliberate debt vs. accrued debt

A tightly-coupled version shipped on purpose to hit a real deadline, with an actual plan to revisit it, is a reasonable trade — the team made an informed choice and knows the cost is temporary. The same code, untouched for two years while three more channels get bolted on the same coupled way, is debt that's accrued real interest: the eventual refactor now has to untangle far more than the original shortcut ever cost.

"Bad code" is a stronger criticism, and "debt" is only used to be polite about it
"Debt" only applies to code with bugs; "bad code" only applies to code without bugs

items.prompt: Implement `cumulativeChangeCost(numChanges, baseCost, couplingPenaltyPercent)`: the cost of the first change is `baseCost`; each subsequent change costs `couplingPenaltyPercent`% more than the previous one. Return the sum of all `numChanges` change costs, rounded to 2 decimal places.

tests.description: 0% penalty gives a flat cost per change (decoupled case)
a single change just costs baseCost
positive penalty compounds across changes

items.explanation: This is literally the function from L3's worked example: at 0% growth every change costs the same as the first (the decoupled OrderService), and at any positive growth rate the cost compounds change over change (the coupled OrderService), matching the diverging curve from L2's chart.
items.reference:
Cost of the Nth change compounds by a fixed percentage under coupling; stays flat at 0% growth (the decoupled case).

items.learnMore:
Modeling the compounding cost curve

L3's `cumulativeChangeCost` function is a small, direct model of the cost curve from L2: each change costs a percentage more than the last (the "coupling penalty"), and the total is the running sum. At 0% penalty it reproduces the decoupled design's flat per-change cost; at any positive penalty it reproduces the coupled design's compounding curve — the higher the penalty, the faster the divergence.
